t: No provision in the appropriations Act for the fiscal year 1996 referred to in section 101 of this joint resolution that makes the availability of any appropriation provided therein dependent upon the enactment of additional authorizing or other legislation shall be effective before the date set forth in section 106(c) of this joint resolution.

fable.w: This provision only governs when certain appropriations contingencies take effect in a continuing resolution. The only actor implicated is Congress (enacting legislation), which is inside the federal government; there is no consultation, comment, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue involving outside parties.
fable.s: dependent upon the enactment of additional authorizing or other legislation

qwen_block.w: This section addresses the timing of the effectiveness of appropriations provisions relative to other legislation. It does not involve any consultation, coordination, or decision-making process involving parties outside the federal government. The actors involved are Congress (via the joint resolution) and the executive branch (via the appropriations act), all of which are inside the federal government.
qwen_block.s: No provision in the appropriations Act for the fiscal year 1996 referred to in section 101 of this joint resolution that makes the availability of any appropriation provided therein dependent upon the enactment of additional authorizing or other legislation shall be effective before the date set forth in section 106(c) of this joint resolution.

opus.w: This is a timing rule in a fiscal year 1996 continuing resolution. It delays the effect of appropriation provisions that depend on further legislation being enacted. Enacting legislation involves only Congress, which is inside the federal government. There is no comment period, hearing, outside advisory body, consultation with non-federal parties, rulemaking, or right to sue.
opus.b: 1. **Reasoning:** One could misread "enactment of additional authorizing or other legislation" as calling for outside input. It doesn't. Passing legislation is something Congress does, and Congress is inside the federal government. The provision only sets when certain appropriation conditions take effect. No one outside the government takes part in any decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section establishes a timing rule for the effectiveness of certain appropriations provisions. It does not require or recommend any consultation, coordination, or participation with parties outside the federal government (such as states, tribes, the public, or private entities). The reference to 'additional authorizing or other legislation' pert to the legislative process within Congress, which is inside the federal government.
qwen_chat.s: No provision in the appropriations Act for the fiscal year 1996 referred to in section 101 of this joint resolution that makes the availability of any appropriation provided therein dependent upon the enactment of additional authorizing or other legislation shall be effective before the date set forth in section 106(c) of this joint resolution.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that making appropriations dependent on "additional authorizing or other legislation" implies a process involving Congress or other entities, but this is a procedural constraint on the timing of funds, not a requirement for outside participation in a decision. The text does not mention any consultation, hearing, comment period, or advisory body involving non-federal actors. It is purely an internal fiscal rule regarding the effective date of appropriations.
